1.title: Impediments, Technical Debt and the Organization
1.text: Welcome to Module 14: Impediments, Technical Debt and the Organization. This is the last topic module, and it applies the Scrum Master's service beyond the team. You will learn how to deal with what blocks the team, what slows the product, and what must change around the team.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Give three organizational impediments and two ways to help the team. Apply one technique to resolve an impediment. Explain the impact of technical debt. Name three practices that raise quality. Describe one organizational design change from adopting Scrum. And say why Scrum has no project manager.

1.title: Case Check-In: Waiting for Others
1.text: At RideLoop, the team waits for others. Ravi's Platform Team takes days to answer requests for the payment test environment. The Architecture Group demands a three-week review before any change to the kiosk firmware. The old firmware slows every change, and defects are rising. You are the Scrum Master, and you ask what is yours to remove, and what belongs to the organization. This module helps you separate the two.

1.title: What an Impediment Is
1.text: An impediment is anything that blocks or slows the team's progress. The Guide makes the Scrum Master accountable for "causing the removal of impediments," and for removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams. Impediments should be raised early; the Daily Scrum surfaces them every working day. And note the accountability: it is for the result. The Scrum Master need not fix every impediment personally.

1.title: Resolving an Impediment
1.text: How do you resolve one? First, make it visible. Second, find the root cause. Third, decide whether the team can resolve it. If yes, the team acts, with the Scrum Master's coaching. If not, the Scrum Master works with the organization and escalates with evidence. Finally, verify that the impediment is gone, and learn from it in the Retrospective. The Guide gives only the accountability, so this method goes beyond it, but it is the pattern behind most impediment questions.

1.title: Two Levels of Impediment
1.text: Impediments live at two levels. At the team level: a broken build, an unclear item, a missing skill, a conflict. The team resolves these, with the Scrum Master's coaching. At the organizational level: people split across projects, slow approvals, no test environment, managers overruling the Product Owner. The Scrum Master works on these with managers and other groups. Telling the team to cope with an organizational impediment is the wrong answer.

1.title: Organizational Impediments
1.text: The learning objective asks for at least three organizational impediments. These go beyond the Guide. People split across several projects, so they cannot focus. Functional silos and hand-offs, so work waits. Slow approvals and gates, so adaptation is delayed. Managers overruling the Product Owner. Command-and-control management, which blocks self-management. Unavailable stakeholders, which delays feedback. Metrics that reward the plan. And missing tools or environments. The Architecture Group's review at RideLoop is an example of a slow gate.

1.title: How the Scrum Master Helps the Team
1.text: At least two ways the Scrum Master helps the team with impediments. These go beyond the Guide. Make the impediment visible: at the Daily Scrum, on a board, with its cost in lost time. Coach the team to resolve what it can. Remove what it cannot, by working with managers and other teams. Find the root cause: look past the symptom. Escalate with evidence. Facilitate a resolution session, bringing the right people together, neutrally. And follow through: check it is gone, and use the Retrospective to stop it coming back.

1.title: Techniques to Resolve an Impediment
1.text: You should be able to apply at least one technique. These techniques go beyond the Guide. The five whys: ask why about five times to find the root cause. A fishbone diagram: group possible causes by people, process, tools, environment and policy. A prioritized impediment board, when there are many. Escalation with data, for organizational impediments. A facilitated working session, when groups must agree. A small experiment, when the solution is unclear. And Retrospective problem-solving, for recurring problems.

1.title: The 5 Whys: A Worked Example
1.text: Here is a worked example of the five whys; it goes beyond the Guide. The Increment is not ready for the Review. Why? Testing was not finished. Why? The shared test environment was down for three days. Why? Another team's load tests were using it. Why? Nobody schedules the shared environment. Why? The organization never assigned it an owner. The root cause is the missing owner. The action: the Scrum Master works with management to assign one, or give the team its own environment, using the three lost days as evidence.

1.title: Technical Debt
1.text: Now technical debt. The Guide does not mention it, but the learning objectives do. It means the future cost of rework from taking an easy shortcut now instead of a better approach. Like financial debt, it carries interest: the longer it stays, the more it costs. The diagram shows the cycle. Shortcuts create debt, debt slows delivery, pressure grows, and more shortcuts follow. A strong Definition of Done and visibility break the cycle.

1.title: The Impact of Accumulating Debt
1.text: What is the impact of accumulating technical debt? The Guide never mentions it, so this list goes beyond the Guide. Delivery gets slower, because every change takes longer. The cost rises, because rework and workarounds eat effort. There are more defects, because fragile parts break. Forecasts become less reliable. The product is harder to adapt to change. Morale falls, because working in a poor code base is frustrating. And the Increment itself may stop being usable. In the exam, name the impact, not the metaphor.

1.title: How Scrum Deals with Debt
1.text: How does Scrum deal with debt? The Guide never mentions it, so this goes beyond the Guide. The Definition of Done is the first defense: unfinished quality is not Done, and quality does not decrease during the Sprint. The debt is made visible, for example as Product Backlog items, so the Product Owner can weigh it against new features. The Developers are accountable for quality, the Product Owner orders the debt work, and the Scrum Master helps everyone see the impact. And there are no separate debt or hardening Sprints.

1.title: Practices That Raise Quality
1.text: Now practices. The learning objective asks for at least three that raise quality. They come from extreme programming and DevOps, not from the Guide. Test-driven development: write a failing test first. Automated testing: fast, repeatable checks. Continuous integration: problems appear early. Continuous delivery: reliable, frequent releases. Refactoring: improve the code before debt grows. Pair and mob programming: shared knowledge and instant review. Code reviews and standards: early defect discovery. And simple design. The Developers choose which to use; the Scrum Master encourages and removes barriers.

1.title: Organizational Design Changes
1.text: Adopting Scrum changes the organization, and the objective asks you to summarize at least one change. These changes go beyond the Guide. Departments become cross-functional product teams. Assigned work becomes self-managing teams. Managers move from controllers to leaders, coaches and enablers. Quality moves from a final department to something built in. And funding moves from fixed projects to products and Product Goals. Managers and project managers are changed the most.

1.title: Why Scrum Has No Project Manager
1.text: Why does Scrum have no project manager? The Guide never mentions the role, so this reasoning goes beyond it. Self-management: the team decides who does what, when and how. There is no hierarchy inside the Scrum Team. Scrum relies on empiricism, not detailed up-front control. The duties are shared among the three accountabilities. And there is one goal, with one Product Backlog and one Product Owner. The skills of project management stay; what does not exist is a role above the team.

1.title: Where Project Management Duties Go
1.text: Where do the duties go? This mapping goes beyond the Guide. Scope and priorities go to the Product Owner. Planning, estimating and quality go to the Developers. Process and impediments go to the Scrum Master. Reporting is replaced by transparency of the artifacts. Nobody assigns tasks, because the Developers decide. And people who used to be project managers can serve as Product Owner, Scrum Master or Developer, or in other roles in the organization.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. The Scrum Master is accountable for removal: not for fixing alone, and not for waiting. Make impediments visible first; waiting for the Retrospective is slow. Organizational impediments need work with the organization. Root cause beats symptom, and the Definition of Done is the main defense against debt. No hardening Sprints, and practices are the Developers' choice. And there is no project manager: nobody assigns tasks or sits above the team. Technical debt is not in the Guide, so answer from its impact.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. For impediments: make them visible, find the cause, and remove them with the right people. For organizational ones, the Scrum Master works with the organization. Debt makes delivery slower, costlier and riskier, and the Definition of Done guards against it. Practices such as automation, integration and refactoring help. The organization moves to product teams, self-management and enabling managers. And there is no project manager. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. An impediment needs a decision from a Lakeshore Transit executive whom the Scrum Master cannot reach directly. What should the Scrum Master do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Make the impediment visible with evidence of its cost, and work with those who can reach the executive. Cancelling a Sprint is for an obsolete Sprint Goal only.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. After adopting Scrum, Lakeshore Transit merges its separate analysis, development and test departments into cross-functional product teams. How is this described? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A, an organizational design change caused by adopting Scrum. Cross-functional teams hold all the skills for an Increment.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Maya wants only new features, while the code base is getting harder to change and defects are rising. What is the best way for the Scrum Master to help? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Make the debt and its impact visible so Maya can weigh it, and keep quality in the Definition of Done. A separate hardening Sprint is not part of Scrum.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which set contains practices that raise quality and reduce technical debt? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B: automated testing, continuous integration and refactoring. They give fast feedback and keep the code clean. The other options add things Scrum does not have, or do not address quality.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Why does Scrum have no project manager? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. The team is self-managing without hierarchy, and the duties are shared among three accountabilities. The Scrum Master does not take the project manager's role, and the Product Owner does not control the Developers' plan.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: C. Make it visible with evidence and work with those who can act. Question two: A. A typical organizational design change. Question three: D. Make the debt visible, and keep quality in the Definition of Done. Question four: B. Automated testing, continuous integration and refactoring. Question five: C. Self-management and shared duties. That completes the topic modules. Next, Module 15 is a scenario workshop.
